report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p > .05", Text = "Returners did not differ from the 186 participants who did not return on any of the 27 Round 1 eye-movement features tested (all p > .05, Mann-Whitney U tests) or in sex distribution (p = .40, χ² test); they were slightly younger (median 20 vs. 21 years, p < .001, rank-biserial r = .22)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

text.text: Saccadic and fixation measures are widely used in psychiatry and neurology, yet no published centile norms exist for expressing a new recording as a centile or deviation score.
We derived norms from GazeBase v2.0 (EyeLink 1000, 1000 Hz, left eye), using Round 1 recordings from 322 healthy young adults aged 18-46, most (284/322) aged 18-25.
Twenty-nine features were extracted from three tasks-horizontal saccades (HSS), random oblique saccades (RAN), and central fixation (FXS).
Norms are empirical centiles (5th-95th).

We tested age and sex effects with generalized additive models for location, scale and shape (GAMLSS), assessed calibration with split-half resampling (50 random splits), and estimated 4-month test-retest reliability in 136 returners (ICC(2,1), absolute agreement).
Median main-saccade latency was 121 ms in predictable HSS and 199 ms in unpredictable RAN, with median peak velocity 527 °/s and 440 °/s, respectively.
Six of the 29 features differed by sex after Benjamini-Hochberg correction (q < .05), notably fixation small-saccade rate (female median 0.27/s vs. male 0.13/s).
text.formatted: Six of the 29 features differed by sex after Benjamini-Hochberg correction (q < .05), notably fixation small-saccade rate (female median 0.27/s vs. male 0.13/s).

text.text: Split-half calibration was near-nominal except for ceiling and floor variables.
Four features had good reliability (ICC ≥ .75), 8 moderate, and 17 poor (ICC < .50); fixation duration and small-saccade amplitude were least reliable (ICC = .11).
text.formatted: Four features had good reliability (ICC ≥ .75), 8 moderate, and 17 poor (ICC < .50); fixation duration and small-saccade amplitude were least reliable (ICC = .11).

text.text: At retest, HSS latency increased systematically (+53.0 ms), whereas RAN latency was unchanged.
The HSS norms are therefore first-exposure norms.
These frozen v1 norms allow new recordings on the same EyeLink tasks to be expressed as centiles and deviation scores, but their clinical validity requires prospective validation in patient samples.
Clinical neuroscience increasingly asks not whether a patient group differs from a control group on average, but where an individual patient falls relative to healthy variation.

Normative modeling formalizes that question: a reference distribution is estimated in healthy individuals, and each new individual is expressed as a centile or deviation (z) score against it (Marquand et al., 2016; Rutherford et al., 2022; Wolfers et al., 2018).

text.text: The approach has produced population brain charts for structural imaging across the lifespan (Bethlehem et al., 2022) -on a far larger scale, with more than 100,000 participants across the lifespan, while the present norms cover 322 young adults over about eight well-supported years -and it is attractive in psychiatry precisely because diagnostic categories are heterogeneous -two patients with the same diagnosis may deviate on entirely different measures, a pattern that group-average comparisons erase.

text.text: Eye movements are a natural candidate for the same treatment.

Saccadic latency, amplitude, gain and peak velocity (the amplitude-peak velocity relation known as the main sequence; Bahill et al., 1975; Gibaldi & Sabatini, 2021), fixation stability and microsaccades (Martinez-Conde et al., 2004) can be quantified with millisecond and sub-degree precision, differ, on average, from healthy values in several psychiatric and neurological conditions (Gooding & Basso, 2008; Hutton & Ettinger, 2006), and can be recorded with identical hardware across sites.

text.text: Yet interpretation still depends on ad hoc control groups: each study recruits its own comparison sample, with its own age range, device settings and feature definitions, so a latency of 210 ms may be unremarkable in one paper and pathological in another.
No published set of centile norms -reference values that allow a new individual recording to be expressed as a centile or deviation score -exists for saccadic and fixation features.

The closest large-sample reference, Bargary et al. (2017), reported normative means, distributions and reliabilities for 21 pro-saccade, anti-saccade and smooth-pursuit measures in 1,058 healthy young adults, but published no centile tables and no scoring procedure, and its measures were derived from different tasks and hardware.

text.text: That study reports test-retest reliabilities for its measures and substantial sex differences, both of which the present norms build on.

It does not, however, provide what a scoring reference requires: it publishes no centile values for any measure, no procedure for expressing a new recording as a centile or deviation score, and no fixation or microsaccade measures, and its recordings were made with different hardware (JAZZ-novo infrared oculography) and a different task battery.

The gap this study addresses is therefore specific: frozen centile norms, with calibration and test-retest reliability, for a defined set of saccadic and fixation features recorded with the EyeLink hardware family used in many clinical laboratories.
GazeBase makes such norms feasible.

It is a public, longitudinal dataset of 12,334 monocular recordings from 322 college-aged participants, collected with an EyeLink 1000 at 1000 Hz over nine rounds spanning 37 months (Griffith et al., 2021).
text.formatted: It is a public, longitudinal dataset of 12,334 monocular recordings from 322 college-aged participants, collected with an EyeLink 1000 at 1000 Hz over nine rounds spanning 37 months <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Griffith et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Its size supports centile estimation, its repeated rounds support test-retest reliability, and because the recordings were made with the same EyeLink hardware family used in many clinical laboratories, norms derived from it can, in principle, be applied to new clinical recordings of the same tasks.

GazeBase has also spawned derived resources, such as AnnotatedGazeBase, which provides annotated and imputed recordings from the random saccade task (Siradj, 2026); the norms reported here are built from the original unimputed recordings.

text.text: This study had three aims: (1) to construct and freeze centile norms for a defined set of saccadic and fixation features from three GazeBase tasks; (2) to validate the norms internally by split-half calibration and to test whether age-or sex-specific norms are required; and (3) to quantify 4-month test-retest reliability feature by feature, so that users know which features were stable over 4 months and which were not.
The study is deliberately methodological: it establishes and validates a measurement reference, and makes no claim about any clinical group.
We used GazeBase v2.0 (Figshare record 12912257; MD5 checksum verified on download).
All recordings are monocular (left eye), sampled at 1000 Hz with an EyeLink 1000 in desktop-mount configuration, with calibration and validation before each task (Griffith et al., 2021).

The normative sample comprises all 322 Round 1 participants: healthy young adults aged 18-46 years (mean 21.9, median 21), 171 male and 151 female.

The age distribution is dense at 18-25 years (n = 284) and sparse above 26 years (n = 38, 1-6 participants per year of age); the norms therefore describe young adults, and this constraint is carried through the interpretation.
Test-retest analyses used the 136 participants who returned for Round 2, approximately 4 months later.

Returners did not differ from the 186 participants who did not return on any of the 27 Round 1 eye-movement features tested (all p > .05, Mann-Whitney U tests) or in sex distribution (p = .40, χ² test); they were slightly younger (median 20 vs. 21 years, p < .001, rank-biserial r = .22).

text.text: Three of the seven GazeBase tasks were used.

In the horizontal saccade task (HSS), the target stepped between ±15° and 0°, giving 100 target steps per recording; step direction and timing are predictable, so the task elicits anticipatory saccades (Joiner & Shelhamer, 2006; Shelhamer & Joiner, 2003).

text.text: In the random saccade task (RAN), the target stepped to unpredictable oblique positions, giving 99 target steps; anticipation is largely impossible.
In the fixation task (FXS), participants fixated a central target for 15 s.
HSS and RAN together provide a consistency check: a correct target-locked pipeline must show far more anticipation in HSS than in RAN, and it did (anticipatory rates 0.41 vs 0.04).

Features were extracted from the EyeLink online parser's event labels (fixation, saccade, blink) rather than from a re-implemented velocity algorithm, so that the pipeline can be applied unchanged to clinical EyeLink recordings exported the same way (for how event-detection approaches differ in their outputs, see Andersson et al., 2017; Holmqvist et al., 2011; Larsson et al., 2013; Nyström & Holmqvist, 2010; Salvucci & Goldberg, 2000).

For each target step in HSS and RAN, the main saccade was defined as the largest saccade within [-300, +600] ms of the step -a window chosen to include anticipatory saccades before the step and the full range of reactive latencies after it, while keeping each saccade assigned to a single step; latency is the interval from step to main-saccade onset and can be negative for anticipatory responses.

text.text: Scoring a new recording.

To score a new same-task EyeLink recording, extract the same 29 features with the same pipeline (gazebase_extract_r12.py), then convert each feature value to a centile and a deviation (z) score against the frozen Round 1 norms (gazebase_zscore.R, provided as supplementary material).

The grid is first mapped to z-scores through the standard normal quantile function, and each value is interpolated linearly in z-space between neighbouring grid points; values outside the grid are extrapolated with the end-segment slope and z is clipped to ±4.
Where Table 3 provides sex-specific norms, the sex-specific grid is used; otherwise the pooled grid is used.

A RAN latency of 199 ms sits exactly on the pooled 50th centile (z = 0.00); scored sex-specifically, the same 199 ms is the 36th centile for a woman (z = -0.36) and the 59th for a man (z = +0.23), because the female median is 204 ms and the male median 195 ms.

Seventeen features were poor (< 0.50); the lowest were FXS fixation duration (0.11) and small-saccade amplitude (0.11-0.16 across tasks).

One poor value requires interpretation rather than alarm: the main-saccade detection rate sits at its ceiling (almost every participant scores 1.0 at both rounds), so there is almost no between-person variance for an ICC to capture.

FXS fixation duration rose by a mean of +230 ms, but the median paired change was only +55 ms (95% CI -88 to +208 ms; Wilcoxon p = .35), and the mean is carried by a few participants with shifts of several seconds; we do not interpret the mean as a group-level change.
The clearest reliability finding is a systematic change, not noise.

In HSS, mean latency increased by 53.0 ms from Round 1 to Round 2 (113.9 to 166.9 ms; p = 1.3 × 10 ¹ ) and the ⁻ ⁰ anticipatory rate fell from 0.41 to 0.26 (p < 0.001); only 71% of Round 2 anticipatory rates fell inside the Round 1 normative interval, the lowest coverage of any feature. 40) is lower than its consistency ICC (0.48): part of the disagreement is the systematic shift itself.

The HSS latency and anticipatory-rate norms in Table 2 are therefore first-exposure norms: they describe a first encounter with the task, not performance after practice.

Discussion This study delivers what eye-movement research in psychiatry has lacked: a frozen, splithalf-calibrated set of reference centiles for saccadic and fixation features, built on 322 healthy young adults recorded with standard clinical hardware, together with an explicit account of which features can support individual-level interpretation.
Three conclusions follow.
First, reliability -not group difference -should decide which features lead a deviationscore analysis.

RAN latency, RAN peak velocity and HSS saccade duration combine good 4month stability with tight normative distributions; they are the features on which an individual's deviation is most likely to reflect a genuine individual difference (cf. Bargary et al., 2017).

text.text: Fixation duration and small-saccade amplitude (see Rolfs, 2009; Rucci & Victor, 2015), by contrast, vary so much within the same person over 4 months that a single-session deviation score on them is mostly a measurement of the day, not of the person -the reliability paradox for individual differences (Hedge et al., 2018).

text.text: They remain legitimate as group-level or exploratory measures, but they should not headline an individual-level claim.
Second, predictability changes what a latency measures.

The disappearance of anticipation at retest -a 53 ms latency shift confined to the predictable task -shows that HSS latency and anticipatory rate index familiarity and strategy as much as oculomotor physiology (for latency as a decision variable, see Carpenter & Williams, 1995).

text.text: Studies that compare a clinical group tested once against norms must therefore match participants on task exposure, or prefer the unpredictable task, whose latency was stable over the 4-month interval studied (ICC 0.75, no mean shift).
This is a concrete, checkable prescription that follows directly from the reliability data -the kind of guidance a norms paper is meant to provide.

For longitudinal use, a follow-up recording should be scored against these first-exposure norms only for features without an exposure effect -the good-reliability features RAN latency, RAN peak velocity, RAN peak velocity for 10-20° saccades and HSS saccade duration are the safest for tracking change; HSS latency and anticipatory rate require an exposure-matched comparison, or the unpredictable task, whose latency showed no exposure shift.

Separating a novelty effect from a lasting practice effect would require retesting at two or more intervals, which the present tworound design cannot do; such retesting is a planned follow-up analysis using the later GazeBase rounds.
Third, sex-specific norms are not optional for six of the features.
A two-fold sex difference in fixation small-saccade rate means that pooled centiles would systematically misclassify one sex.
Table 3 removes that bias for the six affected features; users should treat the stratified table as the default wherever it exists.
Frozen norms and ad hoc local controls serve different purposes.

Frozen norms give every new recording the same reference, so deviation scores are comparable across studies and sites; they are preferable when the aim is individual-level scoring or cross-study comparison and the new sample matches the norm sample (young adults, EyeLink 1000, same tasks).

A local control group is preferable when the new sample differs from the norm sample in age, hardware or task parameters, or when the research question is a group contrast within a single study; local controls also absorb site-specific calibration and setting differences that frozen norms cannot.
The two are complementary: a study can report deviation scores against the frozen norms and, where a local control group exists, check that the same pattern appears against it.

The intended use of these norms is prospective: a new participant -in our program, a patient and a matched control recorded on an EyeLink with the same three tasks -is scored against the frozen centiles, yielding a profile of deviation scores across features rather than a single group contrast.

Whether such profiles carry clinical information (for example, separating first-episode patients from healthy individuals, or tracking change in features without exposure effects) is an empirical question for the clinical study, and we deliberately do not prejudge it here.
Normative references in neuroimaging followed this sequence: the reference and its validation came first, clinical applications second (Marquand et al., 2016; Bethlehem et al., 2022).

The 4-month retest interval makes the reliability estimates conservativeshort-interval reliability will be higher -but it also means genuinely state-sensitive features cannot be distinguished from noisy ones on these data alone.

Small-saccade features rest on the EyeLink parser's segments with a 2° amplitude cut-off (the authors' operational cut-off, not a literature microsaccade criterion) and are not equivalent to microsaccades as defined by dedicated detection algorithms (Engbert & Mergenthaler, 2006; Otero-Millan et al., 2008 , 2014); 48 of 322 participants produced no FXS small saccade at all.

text.text: Finally, this is a methodological reference study: it contains no clinical sample, and no statement in it should be read as evidence that deviation scores diagnose or predict any disorder.

One further caveat: the retest subsample was slightly younger than those who did not return (median 20 vs. 21 years), so the reliability estimates may generalize most directly to younger adults; the two groups did not differ on any baseline eye-movement measure, however, which argues against substantial selection bias in the retest estimates.

Centile norms for 29 saccadic and fixation features, with near-nominal split-half calibration, sex-stratified values where required, and feature-level 4-month reliability, are now available as a frozen reference for EyeLink recordings of the HSS, RAN and FXS tasks in young adults.

The reliability gradient across features -RAN saccade metrics that were stable over 4 months at one end, exposure-sensitive anticipation and unstable fixation-duration and smallsaccade-amplitude measures at the other -is itself a result: it tells future clinical studies where individual-level signal can plausibly be found.     2). 95% confidence intervals for the mean differences are given in the table; Pearson r, Bland-Altman limits of agreement, paired t-statistics and median paired differences are in Supplementary Table S3.

We searched PubMed and the general web on 12 November 2026 for prior eyemovement norms (search terms: GazeBase AND (norm* OR percentile OR reference values)), covering works that used the GazeBase database and published oculomotor norms from selfrecruited samples.
No published percentile norm based on GazeBase was found.

The closest prior works were Hopf et al. (2018; n = 100, mean ± SD only, no percentile norms, retest, fixation or microsaccade measures), the OCAT norms (Journal of Eye Movement Research, 2026-10-02; n = 350, regression-based reference intervals and z-scores, no percentile norms or retest), and OMAT (2021; saccades-per-minute clinical screening norm).
GazeBase itself had previously been used mainly for biometrics and algorithm validation.

One in-press Scientific Reports article models saccade-plus-pupil dynamics on GazeBase HSS data (n = 242) and mentions reference values but provides no percentile norm; a 2025 University of Oslo master's project page describes planned GazeBase norms but is not a publication.
